Some good man must be chosen by us and always kept before our eyes, so that we may always live as if he were looking on, and do all things as if he saw. A great part of sins is taken away if a witness to be revered stands by one who is about to sin.

paras.t: Præterea, in isto capitulo, ad evitandum sollicite omnem detractionem instruimur. Quocirca pensandum quia, ut ait Thomas in secunda secundæ, quæstione 73, Sicut quis nocet alteri facto dupliciter, scilicet manifeste, ut in violentia et rapina, et secrete, sicut in furto ; sic unus nocet alteri verbis duobus modis : primo occulte, ut in detractione ; secundo aperte, sicut in contumelia. Dicitur autem homo detrahere, non quia semper aliquid minuat de veritate, sed quoniam quantum in se est, intendit bonitatem famæ alterius minorare directe aut indirecte. Directe, quatuor modis : primo, dum alteri falsum imponit ; secundo, dum culpam ejus exaggerat seu adauget ; tertio, dum revelat occulta ; quarto, dum ea quæ bona sunt, affirmat prava intentione peracta. Indirecte quoque dupliciter : primo, dum negat bonum alterius ; secundo, dum malitiose reticet illud. At vero quam grave sit crimen detractio, constat ex hoc, quod Apostolus ad Romanos, detractores vocat odibiles Deo. Et item ex hoc, quod, ut refert S. Clemens, beatissimus princeps Apostolorum asseruit esse tria homicidii genera. Primum est homicidium corporale. Secundum est odium : nam in prima Canonica sua ait Joannes, Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est. Tertium, detractio : de qua testatur Bernardus, quod sit gladius ex utraque parte acutus, interficiens tam animam detrahentis, quam mentem audientis. Hinc de S. Pacomio legitur, quod quum audiret aliquem detrahentem, protinus fugit ab illo tanquam a basilisco.
paras.en: Further, in this chapter we are taught to avoid carefully all detraction. Wherefore we must consider that, as Thomas says in the Secunda Secundae, question 73: Just as one harms another by deed in two ways, namely openly, as in violence and robbery, and secretly, as in theft; so one harms another by words in two ways: first secretly, as in detraction; secondly openly, as in contumely [that is, insult to a man's face]. Now a man is said to detract, not because he always takes something from the truth, but because, as far as in him lies, he intends to lessen the good of another's reputation, directly or indirectly. Directly, in four ways: first, when he imputes something false to another; secondly, when he exaggerates or increases his fault; thirdly, when he reveals hidden things; fourthly, when he asserts that things which are good were done with an evil intention. Indirectly also in two ways: first, when he denies another's good; secondly, when he maliciously keeps silent about it. But how grave a crime detraction is appears from this, that the Apostle, writing to the Romans, calls detractors hateful to God[[Rom 1:30||]]. And also from this, that, as St. Clement relates, the most blessed prince of the Apostles declared that there are three kinds of homicide. The first is bodily homicide. The second is hatred: for John says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:15|Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer|Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est]]. The third, detraction: of which Bernard testifies that it is a sword sharp on both sides, killing both the soul of the detractor and the mind of the hearer. Hence we read of St. Pachomius that when he heard anyone detracting, he at once fled from him as from a basilisk.

paras.t: Postremo hortatur nos scriptura hujus capituli, ut in omnibus simus considerati et circumspecti, et ex prudenti deliberatione procedamus in actum. Nempe, ut ait Bernardus, consideratio mentem purificat, regit affectus, dirigit actus, corrigitque excessus ; mores componit, vitam ordinat et honestat.
paras.en: Lastly, the text of this chapter exhorts us to be considerate and circumspect in all things, and to proceed to action from prudent deliberation. For, as Bernard says, consideration purifies the mind, rules the affections, directs the acts and corrects excesses; it composes the manners, orders the life and makes it honourable.
